Other notable lines that have tested or started transport include the Alstom Coradia iLint passenger line in Quebec, Canada in September 2023 [2], the Stadler commuter FLIRT H2 line running through San Bernadino, California in 2024 [3], and the CPKC hydrogen coal-freight locomotive in British Columbia, Canada in 2024 [4]. Since the beginning of hydrogen transport technology development, much work has been devoted to risk and safety analysis of these systems. Quantitative and qualitative safety research has been performed to better elucidate the unique hazards of hydrogen fuel cell systems compared to internal combustion engines. Recently, more attention has been given to requirements for building or retrofitting rail maintenance facilities for cost-effective and safe operation. The adoption of hydrogen rail has driven a critical need for clear guidelines regarding ventilation requirements, setback distances, and indoor storage limits for maintenance facilities. This has necessitated a closer evaluation of the unique requirements and potential hazards for large hydrogen rail systems in enclosed facilities. Several national government agencies and research groups have been evaluating the safety and regulations related to hydrogen rail systems and fuel cell maintenance service facilities. A 2009 failure modes and effects analysis (FMEA) of hydrogen fuel cell vehicles showed that the greatest hazard for such systems are large releases of hydrogen, such as from the failure of temperature and pressure relief devices to open or from a rupture of the fuel tank, and that single point failures that lead to such a release should be avoided [5]. Building on this work, an FMEA of hydrogen locomotive on-board components determined that higher risk scenarios are associated with leaks from tanks, fuel lines, valves, the engine, and pumps. This work suggested using solenoid shut-off valves, ensuring tank integrity, and designing systems for easy access by first responders as potential mitigation measures [6]. Likewise, a hazard analysis for hydrogen rail performed by Transport Canada in 2022 also determined that the greatest risk is posed by tank rupture, especially in areas where people are present, and that countermeasures such as fire detection, multiple temperature and pressure relief devices (TPRDs), and thermal protection for tanks should be employed [7]. Relatedly, a 2025 HAZOP study of maintenance of fuel cell electric buses has shown that improper electrical grounding, faulty pressure and level sensor monitoring, and human errors are higher- priority modes that may result in hydrogen release and ignition [8]. Another HAZOP and risk assessment study performed in 2020 of hydrogen vehicles in repair garages identified failures such as opening of the TPRD due to overheating, premature disconnect of the venting/defueling tool, and small, low-pressure releases as hazardous scenarios [9, 10]. Also, a 2024 quantitative risk assessment of hydrogen-powered locomotives showed that individual fatality risk was most sensitive to fires from full bore leaks (those that are size-equivalent to 100% of the cross section of the pipe) and that pipe size, leak detection capability, and component leak likelihood greatly affect risk outcomes [11].
